title: CHAPTER EIGHT. On the ceremonial law: definition
english: CHAPTER EIGHT. On the ceremonial law.

After the moral law follows the CEREMONIAL, which is an ordinance of God containing precepts concerning the external worship of God to be observed in the Old Testament Church, for signifying, prefiguring, and sealing the promised good, and for preserving the sworn order in ecclesiastical assemblies and actions.
By this law God's Church in the Old Testament was governed as an infant and a girl under elemental mysteries (Gal. 4:1-3; Heb. 8:5; 10:1; Col. 2:14, 11).

title: II. Four classes of ceremonial precepts; sacrifices divided
english: II. Its precepts, however varied, may chiefly be referred to four classes: sacraments, sacrifices, sacred things, and legal observances. Of the sacraments we will speak below in their place.

A sacrifice is an external sacred action by which some sensible, permanent thing is offered immediately to God by a properly authorized ministerized minister, to testify His supreme dominion and the human's subjection. four ways: by matter, by form, by bloody or unbloody offering, and by particular end (latreutic, eucharistic, petitionary, or propitiatory).

By sacred things are meant sacred persons and all else required for external worship. Legal observances were ceremonies of pacification and sanctification by which they were distinguished from unbelievers.

title: III–IV. Use of the ceremonial law
english: III. The use and abrogation of the ceremonial law are to be observed. IV. Its use was: 1. to hold the ancient people under hope of the promised goods; 2. to distinguish Israel from the nations by a middle wall until Christ tore it down and they coalesced into one body; 3. that occupied with this laborious worship they might neither invent other cults nor take up those invented by others.
The first use it performs through types, figures, and shadows. In this respect that law is rightly called a pedagogue to Christ (Heb. 10:1-3; Col. 2:14, 17; Gal. 3:24; Eph. 2:14-15).

title: V. Abrogation through Christ's cross; Cap.9 next
english: V. The ceremonial law was abrogated through Christ's cross, death, resurrection, ascension, and the sending of the Spirit—by the sun driving away the shadows and the body succeeding into their place.

It is abrogated as to the necessity of observing it, every right of obligation being taken away at once; and by this it ceases to be living and is dead. It was abolished in fact partly by the Apostles' teaching and partly by God's destruction of Jerusalem and the temple. From then those ceremonies became deadly which had been tolerable only among Jews in the intervening space (Col. 2:11-17; Gal. 4:9-10; Acts 16:3; 21:22-24).
CHAPTER NINE follows, On the forensic law.
